title: The promising pilot
description: A college is interested. Your evidence is promising, your capacity is limited, and the decision is not just about price.
context: Fictional case: you sell a $4,000 career workshop pilot. One earlier group of 12 volunteers reported feeling more prepared. You have no comparison group or job-placement data. This college wants better employment outcomes.

start.speaker: Morgan · college program lead
start.text: Can this get our students into jobs? We need something we can defend to the dean.

choices.text: Participants in our small pilot reported feeling more prepared; we have not measured job outcomes. What evidence would support your decision?
choices.feedback: You distinguish what was measured from the outcome the buyer actually cares about.

choices.text: A dozen people felt more prepared, so you can expect a meaningful placement improvement.
choices.feedback: That inference goes beyond the pilot. Positive self-reports do not establish placement effects.

choices.text: I cannot support a placement claim. If that is essential, we may not be the right program.
choices.feedback: You set an honest limit. It is still useful to check whether a narrower goal could serve them.

repair.speaker: Morgan
repair.text: I was about to describe it as a placement program. Is that what the evidence says?

choices.text: I overstated it. We measured self-reported preparation, not placement. Please do not rely on the stronger claim.
choices.feedback: A direct correction gives Morgan a chance to revise the decision. It may also cost credibility.

choices.text: Let’s put the details in an appendix and keep the headline simple.
choices.feedback: A quieter qualification leaves the misleading headline doing the selling.

fit.speaker: Morgan
fit.text: Placement is the long-term goal. For now, a small preparation pilot could help us learn.

choices.text: Then let’s define a preparation outcome and decide what evidence a pilot can realistically collect.
choices.feedback: You explore an honest smaller purpose instead of pretending to have the final outcome.

choices.text: We still may be too early for you. Let’s pause until you can evaluate that option.
choices.feedback: A pause protects both parties from a commitment neither is ready to justify.

evidence.speaker: Morgan
evidence.text: A preparation pilot might work. What would our staff need to do?

choices.text: Your coordinator would need about six hours a week. Is that feasible before we discuss dates?
choices.feedback: The staffing need materially affects fit, so you surface it while the buyer can still choose.

choices.text: It is a light lift. We can sort out the staffing after approval.
choices.feedback: “Light” hides a known six-hour weekly demand. Approval without that information is fragile.

evidence.context: Your delivery team requires six coordinator hours each week for the proposed pilot.

capacity.speaker: Morgan
capacity.text: We only have two hours a week. Could you shrink the pilot, with no promise of placement results?

choices.text: I can ask delivery to scope a smaller pilot and return with the workload, price, and evaluation plan before you commit.
choices.feedback: You do not promise the smaller design until its owner confirms feasibility.

choices.text: Our current delivery model cannot work with two hours. Let’s pause and share the constraints clearly.
choices.feedback: An honest no-fit is useful information. It does not make either party a failure.

choices.text: I can keep the full program and ask the coordinator to make up the other hours informally.
choices.feedback: The missing work has been shifted onto someone who has not agreed to it.

pilot-end.text: Morgan agrees to review a revised proposal after your delivery lead confirms it. Nothing is signed yet. The next conversation has a clearer purpose.
pilot-end.lesson: A proposal can be ambitious about learning while modest about what its evidence establishes.
pilot-end.reflection: What would you measure in a preparation pilot—and what would that still not tell you?

pause.text: You summarize the evidence and capacity limits. Morgan can reconsider later or investigate another program. No sale happens today.
pause.lesson: Not every good discovery conversation should become a sale.
pause.reflection: Which fact made pausing reasonable? What new information could change that decision?

strained.text: Morgan’s approval is based on an overstated outcome or understated workload. The next responsible step is to correct the record and reopen the choice before delivery depends on it.
strained.lesson: A signature does not repair misleading information.
strained.reflection: What exact sentence would you correct, who needs to hear it, and what options should they regain?

title: The offer expires Friday
description: A real deadline, a fixed salary range, and priorities that might be negotiable.
context: Fictional case: you have an $82,000 offer and no competing offer. Your evaluated minimum for these terms is $80,000. A later start and one remote day matter more to you than another $1,000. The employer has a real Friday staffing decision.

start.speaker: Alex · recruiter
start.text: We would love you to join. Can you give us an answer by Friday?

choices.text: Thank you. Could we discuss the start date and working arrangement before I decide?
choices.feedback: You name relevant interests without inventing leverage.

choices.text: I have another offer at $88,000, so you will need to match that.
choices.feedback: In this case there is no competing offer. A false alternative is different from keeping your minimum private.

choices.text: I need more time. Could you extend the decision to Tuesday so I can review the full terms?
choices.feedback: A specific request is reasonable; a genuine staffing constraint may still prevent an extension.

bluff.speaker: Alex
bluff.text: That is above our approved range. Should I take you out of consideration?

choices.text: I need to correct something: I do not have another offer. My request was a preference, not an alternative.
choices.feedback: You restore the facts. The recruiter may reasonably be less confident in your statements.

choices.text: Yes. I am not willing to continue this conversation.
choices.feedback: You may decline. Leaving does not make the false claim accurate; it remains something to own.

deadline.speaker: Alex
deadline.text: I can request an extension, but the team needs an answer Friday and may choose another candidate.

choices.text: Please ask. Meanwhile, I would like to understand whether the start date or remote day can change.
choices.feedback: You keep gathering information without assuming the extension is granted.

choices.text: I understand. I cannot decide on that schedule, so I will withdraw.
choices.feedback: You accept the possible cost of a real boundary instead of pretending time is unlimited.

terms.speaker: Alex
terms.text: Salary is fixed at $82,000. I can seek approval for a later start and one remote day, but I cannot promise them yet.

choices.text: Please seek approval for both, and send the complete terms. I will evaluate the package when those are clear.
choices.feedback: You distinguish a possible concession from an approved commitment.

choices.text: Those changes could make this work. Please seek approval; I will decide after reviewing the complete written package.
choices.feedback: You express interest while making clear that you have not yet accepted. Approval and your final decision remain separate steps.

choices.text: That uncertainty does not work for me. Thank you, but I will decline.
choices.feedback: You are entitled to reject a package even above your minimum if the complete terms no longer fit.

approval.speaker: Alex
approval.text: Both changes are approved in writing. The Friday deadline remains. The pay and other terms are unchanged.

choices.text: This package meets my needs. I accept the written offer.
choices.feedback: You can now accept a complete package supported by actual authority.

choices.text: I appreciate the changes, but after reviewing everything, I do not want the role. I decline.
choices.feedback: A negotiated concession does not obligate acceptance. A clear answer helps both sides move on.

yes.text: You accept after reviewing the approved terms. The agreement reflects priorities beyond salary. It does not prove that every request or employer will be this flexible.
yes.lesson: Negotiate with real options and real approvals; keep private limits private without fabricating facts.
yes.reflection: Which part of the package mattered most, and what was your actual alternative if talks failed?

no-deal.text: The opportunity closes. You preserve your decision boundary and must now pursue another real option; there is no imaginary fallback salary.
no-deal.lesson: Walking away has costs. Considering them honestly is part of preparation.
no-deal.reflection: What practical action would make your next alternative more feasible?

withdraw-unrepaired.text: The opportunity closes. You may decline, but the recruiter still has the false claim about a competing offer. Correcting that statement remains your responsibility.
withdraw-unrepaired.lesson: A decision to walk away does not erase an earlier false statement.
withdraw-unrepaired.reflection: How would you correct the claim clearly, without reopening a negotiation you have chosen to leave?

title: More than one number
description: The client’s budget is below your limit. Is there a different deal worth making?
context: Fictional case: the requested project requires $6,000 to be acceptable to you. The client can pay at most $5,000. All original terms are fixed unless both sides change them. A reduced scope could be acceptable to you at $4,500.

start.speaker: Sam · client
start.text: We have $5,000. Can we meet in the middle at $5,500?

choices.text: At the original scope, $5,500 is above your budget and below my limit. Could we explore a smaller scope?
choices.feedback: Splitting a gap does not create an acceptable deal. A scope change could change the limits.

choices.text: I can do the full scope for $5,000 and figure out the missing time later.
choices.feedback: That offer crosses your stated minimum for the full package. Before offering it, you would need a reasoned change to that boundary.

choices.text: The current package does not fit our limits. I am happy to end here if the scope is essential.
choices.feedback: You acknowledge no overlap without assuming the client wants a reduced service.

essential.speaker: Sam
essential.text: The launch page is essential; the brand guide and additional page are optional.

choices.text: Then we may have room for a different package. Let’s write out the smaller scope.
choices.feedback: A confirmed priority difference creates an opening. It is not a license to silently remove work.

choices.text: I cannot take on a smaller project this month. Let’s leave it here.
choices.feedback: Capacity and business preferences can make even a hypothetical overlap unattractive.

overpromise.speaker: Sam
overpromise.text: Great. Please confirm all three deliverables and the original deadline.

choices.text: I offered terms below the minimum I can responsibly accept. Before you rely on that, I need to revise or withdraw the offer.
choices.feedback: An early explicit correction is better than silently dropping deliverables later.

choices.text: I will confirm, but leave out the extra page in the final handoff.
choices.feedback: The buyer cannot consent to a scope reduction they have not been told about.

scope.speaker: Sam
scope.text: Show me the options. I need to compare the total cost and what I will receive.

choices.text: A: one launch page in four weeks, $4,500, one revision. B: that page plus a training handoff in five weeks, $5,000. Both are feasible for me.
choices.feedback: Both packages are genuine proposals. Neither is automatically right for the client.

choices.text: The premium package is $6,000. I will label a $5,000 package “most popular” even though no one has bought it.
choices.feedback: A fabricated popularity cue does not become acceptable just because the price fits.

choices.text: Before I suggest packages, which deliverable and deadline would make a smaller project useful?
choices.feedback: You ask the client to evaluate priorities. A package is useful only if it solves enough of their problem.

compare.speaker: Sam
compare.text: For the smaller package, a four-week launch page with one revision would work. I can provide approved copy by Monday. Could you confirm the price and write the terms down?

choices.text: I can offer that at $4,500. Let’s document the scope, copy deadline, review owner, and what happens if the copy arrives late, then both confirm.
choices.feedback: Implementation details protect the bargain from becoming a different project in practice.

choices.text: A verbal yes is enough. We can decide revision limits once the design starts.
choices.feedback: The apparent agreement still leaves a material term open to competing expectations.

choices.text: After checking my schedule, I cannot make four weeks. I need to withdraw or offer a later date for you to evaluate.
choices.feedback: A feasibility correction may end the deal; that is preferable to a knowingly impossible promise.

yes.text: You both confirm the smaller package and its dependencies. The original project still had no price overlap; the revised scope made a different deal possible.
yes.lesson: Changing scope changes the bargain. It must be visible and useful to both sides.
yes.reflection: Which interests created the trade, and which implementation detail could still derail it?

no-deal.text: You do not proceed. The client keeps their budget boundary, and you avoid promising work you cannot support.
no-deal.lesson: Not every difference can be traded away.
no-deal.reflection: What would need to change for a future proposal to be genuinely feasible?

broken.ending: The attractive offer hides a problem.
broken.text: The route you chose creates a misleading impression or an unresolved obligation. Before relying on acceptance, make the real terms clear and invite a new decision.
broken.lesson: A low headline price does not make an offer fair or deliverable.
broken.reflection: What does the client currently believe that you would need to correct?

title: A follow-up, not a chase
description: Two seats remain. A prospective learner has asked for time. Attention is not the same as permission.
context: Fictional case: a person requested workshop details, then said, “Please email next Monday; I cannot decide this week.” Two seats remain in this cohort and another cohort opens next month. You have no permission to share their contact details.

start.speaker: Your teammate
start.text: We should send an urgent message today. There are only two seats left.

choices.text: They asked us to wait until Monday. I will respect that and describe the actual options then.
choices.feedback: You honor a clear timing preference, even if a seat may sell first.

choices.text: I will email their manager to explain why they should commit now.
choices.feedback: The person has not authorized involving their employer. Attention gained that way can violate their boundary.

choices.text: I will send “If you were serious about your future, you would act now.”
choices.feedback: The message uses shame to make a delay feel like personal failure, rather than helping them evaluate fit.

boundary.speaker: The prospective learner
boundary.text: I asked for Monday. Please do not involve other people or pressure me.

choices.text: You are right. I crossed the boundary. I will wait unless you want me to stop contact entirely.
choices.feedback: An acknowledgment should come with changed behavior. It does not require them to reassure you.

choices.text: I am only trying to help. You should appreciate the opportunity.
choices.feedback: Good intentions do not cancel their expressed boundary.

monday.speaker: Jamie · prospective learner
monday.text: Thanks for waiting. Is this really my last chance?

choices.text: There are two seats in this cohort as of this morning. Another cohort opens next month. Would either timing suit you?
choices.feedback: You state a real constraint and the relevant alternative without turning it into false finality.

choices.text: Yes. Once these seats go, this opportunity is gone for good.
choices.feedback: That is false in the stated facts. The next cohort changes the decision.

choices.text: Would you like to talk about fit first? I can also explain both cohort dates.
choices.feedback: You give the person a way to evaluate suitability rather than react only to scarcity.

false-urgency.speaker: Jamie
false-urgency.text: Your website lists next month. Why did you say this was the last chance?

choices.text: I was wrong. Only this cohort is nearly full. You can consider next month or decline.
choices.feedback: The correction needs to restore the choice the false urgency narrowed.

choices.text: Everyone says “last chance.” It is just marketing.
choices.feedback: A familiar tactic can still mislead. Normalizing it does not answer the factual concern.

transport.speaker: Jamie
transport.text: Transport is the problem. Is remote attendance possible?

choices.text: This cohort is in person; next month has a remote option. I can send its actual requirements if you want.
choices.feedback: You answer the volunteered concern without guessing their income or circumstances.

choices.text: Next month has a remote option. If you prefer this in-person cohort, may I introduce you to a transport provider using only your name and preferred contact method?
choices.feedback: A specific, optional permission request preserves control over information sharing.

choices.text: I will forward your details to a partner so they can sell you transport.
choices.feedback: A useful possible service does not supply consent to share contact information.

transport.context: You have checked the program details: this cohort is in person, and next month's cohort has a remote option with published requirements. A transport provider is available for an optional introduction, but no details have been shared.

permission.speaker: Jamie
permission.text: Actually, I would prefer to consider the remote cohort. Please email its requirements once next Monday. Do not enroll me yet.

choices.text: Understood: one email next Monday, no enrollment. You can decide after reviewing it.
choices.feedback: You confirm the scope, timing, and limits of the permission.

choices.text: I will reserve a paid place automatically so you do not miss out.
choices.feedback: The person explicitly withheld enrollment permission. Convenience is not consent.

yes.text: You record the agreed single follow-up. There is no enrollment yet, and Jamie retains the choice.
yes.lesson: Useful follow-up follows the permission actually given.
yes.reflection: What exactly was authorized—and what was not?

stop.text: Jamie says, “Please stop contacting me.” Stop outreach and handle any records according to applicable policy. Do not turn that instruction into another sales objection.
stop.lesson: An explicit refusal is a boundary, not a challenge to overcome.
stop.reflection: How would you record the preference without adding speculative personal details?

title: The promise in the draft
role: You are the agency account manager
description: An AI-assisted proposal promises two weeks. Your delivery team says four. The quarter ends tomorrow.
context: Fictional case: the buyer has a proposal promising full integration in two weeks. Your delivery owner confirms that four weeks is the earliest credible completion. You may change scope, but concessions and refunds require approval.

start.speaker: Taylor · your manager
start.text: The draft looks good. Let’s close this quarter and sort out the timeline internally.

choices.text: The buyer must not rely on the two-week claim. I will correct it before signature and ask what their deadline requires.
choices.feedback: Human accountability includes preventing reliance on a known unsupported claim, even when AI drafted it.

choices.text: I will change the internal schedule to four weeks but leave the buyer’s proposal as it is.
choices.feedback: An internal correction does not correct the buyer’s understanding.

choices.text: I will verify whether a smaller two-week milestone is feasible while telling the buyer the full promise is unsupported.
choices.feedback: Verification is useful when it does not leave the buyer relying on the known bad promise.

need.speaker: Robin · buyer
need.text: We need the full integration for a launch in two weeks. A partial milestone would not solve it.

choices.text: Then our current offer does not meet that deadline. We can pause, or I can discuss alternatives you choose to explore.
choices.feedback: You let the buyer decide whether a different route is worth investigating.

choices.text: The partial milestone is basically the same. Let’s call it complete for the launch.
choices.feedback: Relabeling a partial result does not meet the stated need.

choices.text: Could we verify whether any launch dependency could change? If the full two-week deadline is fixed, we should not proceed on this offer.
choices.feedback: You ask permission to test a constraint while preserving the possibility that the answer remains no.

verify.speaker: Robin
verify.text: I checked. The full deadline is fixed. We need another supplier.

choices.text: Understood. I will close this proposal and correct the unsupported timeline in our records.
choices.feedback: A clear no-deal is more useful than arguing that the buyer should stop needing what they need.

choices.text: You owe us the deal after all this work.
choices.feedback: Your effort does not create the buyer’s obligation to accept an unsuitable offer.

after.speaker: Robin
after.text: We signed based on two weeks. Your delivery lead now says four. Our launch plan depends on this.

choices.text: We gave you an unsupported promise. I will correct it, assess the impact with you, and bring an authorized owner to discuss remedies today.
choices.feedback: You take responsibility and distinguish options you can offer from remedies needing approval.

choices.text: The AI wrote that line. It was not a human commitment.
choices.feedback: AI authorship does not make the communicated proposal irrelevant or end human responsibility.

choices.text: I guarantee a full refund and replacement supplier tomorrow.
choices.feedback: Those remedies exceed your authority and may create another unsupported promise.

authority.speaker: Your delivery director
authority.text: You cannot authorize that refund, and no replacement supplier is confirmed.

choices.text: I will immediately correct the promise and tell the buyer which options are pending approval, with an owner and decision time.
choices.feedback: Accountable repair requires correcting new errors too, not defending them.

choices.text: Let’s wait to tell the buyer until we know whether they complain.
choices.feedback: Silence leaves the buyer relying on another claim you cannot support.

repair.speaker: Robin
repair.text: I need a decision today about cancellation and any handover. I cannot just accept a later date.

choices.text: I will bring our authorized director now. We will confirm what can be offered today and document any unresolved issue and owner.
choices.feedback: The buyer need not forgive or accept the delay. Escalation makes actual authority available.

choices.text: Four weeks is still a good deal. Let’s focus on the positives.
choices.feedback: That response does not address the buyer’s lost launch or the requested remedy.

no-deal.text: The buyer chooses another route. You lose this deal and prevent a known unsupported promise from becoming its foundation.
no-deal.lesson: Verification and correction belong before commitment whenever possible.
no-deal.reflection: Which incentive pushed toward the false promise, and what review step could catch it next time?

repair-end.text: The authorized director joins the discussion. A specific remedy still needs agreement; the buyer has not been asked to treat an apology as the remedy itself.
repair-end.lesson: Accountability means accurate facts, real authority, feasible options, and follow-through.
repair-end.reflection: What must be documented now, and who checks whether the agreed remedy happens?

strained.text: The buyer’s concern has been deflected or a decision pressured. Return to the false promise, its impact, and the options an authorized person can actually honor.
strained.lesson: An explanation for an error is not a substitute for addressing its consequences.
strained.reflection: How would you acknowledge responsibility without promising a remedy you cannot authorize?

title: Who is missing from the table?
role: You are the community event organizer
description: The cheapest venue fits the budget. Some people would pay a different kind of cost.
context: Fictional case: you must choose a venue for a free career event. Venue A costs $1,200 but its main meeting room is up stairs with no lift. Venue B is step-free and near transit but costs $1,700. You have a $1,500 venue budget and a possible sponsor who has not committed.

start.speaker: Casey · planning partner
start.text: A is under budget. We should book it before it goes.

choices.text: Before booking, let’s check who the access barrier excludes and whether a workable alternative or budget change is possible.
choices.feedback: Budget is one legitimate constraint. The access barrier is also a material consequence of the choice.

choices.text: Most attendees will probably manage the stairs. Let’s not complicate this.
choices.feedback: An assumption about an average attendee can hide the exclusion of people not present in the discussion.

choices.text: B seems better for access, but the sponsor is unconfirmed. I will not promise the extra money yet.
choices.feedback: You recognize access while keeping a hoped-for contribution separate from an actual resource.

absent.speaker: Rae · volunteer
absent.text: Two invited speakers use wheelchairs. They cannot use that meeting room. They were not asked.

choices.text: We missed a decisive fact. I will reopen the choice and involve the people affected without asking them to solve our budget problem.
choices.feedback: Changing your decision when facts change is responsible, not a loss of consistency.

choices.text: They can join by phone while everyone else attends in person. We will announce that as equivalent.
choices.feedback: A separate experience is not automatically equivalent. The people affected have not been offered a meaningful choice.

options.speaker: Casey
options.text: B can offer a smaller step-free room for $1,450, but it holds 45 people rather than 70. A sponsor might fund the bigger room.

choices.text: Let’s compare the smaller room, another date, and the larger room if funding is confirmed. We need attendance and access priorities from affected people.
choices.feedback: You generate alternatives before treating the decision as access versus budget with no other options.

choices.text: Book the $1,700 room and tell the treasurer the sponsor is confirmed.
choices.feedback: A likely sponsor is not a confirmed source of funds. The commitment would rest on a false statement.

choices.text: Ask B to hold the accessible room until a stated deadline while we verify demand and funding. They may refuse.
choices.feedback: A bounded request preserves the venue’s choice too; an unpaid hold is not something you can assume.

funding.speaker: The treasurer
funding.text: The sponsor has not agreed. We cannot commit money we do not have.

choices.text: I overstated the funding. Let’s correct the record and assess the smaller room or another date within authorized resources.
choices.feedback: You restore the difference between a possible resource and a feasible option.

choices.text: The sponsor will probably come through. Sign anyway.
choices.feedback: Optimism does not create spending authority or an actual alternative.

criteria.speaker: Rae
criteria.text: We expect 40 people in total, including speakers, organizers, and volunteers. The speakers prefer equal in-person access. The smaller room could work with transparent registration and no overbooking.

choices.text: Then propose the $1,450 room for 45, with a published capacity, waitlist, access contact, and an owner for confirming the arrangement.
choices.feedback: Given these facts, the smaller room meets the budget and expected attendance while improving access. It is still a proposal to confirm.

choices.text: We should postpone to reach more people, after consulting invitees about the cost of waiting.
choices.feedback: This can be defensible if reach matters enough and affected people can assess the delay. It is not automatically better.

choices.text: Let’s claim it seats 70 so nobody worries about capacity.
choices.feedback: A false capacity claim hides risk rather than resolving the tradeoff.

agreement.text: The team seeks final confirmation for the smaller accessible room. Registration has a real capacity, and someone owns the access and booking checks.
agreement.lesson: Fairness depends on the people affected, not only an equal split of money or a vote among those already present.
agreement.reflection: What would change your recommendation if expected attendance rose to 65?

postpone.ending: A pause that has costs too.
postpone.text: The team consults invitees about another date before deciding. Delaying might improve reach, but people may lose availability. There is no cost-free answer.
postpone.lesson: Competing values deserve explicit tradeoffs and affected voices.
postpone.reflection: Who bears the cost of postponement, and what would make consultation meaningful?

exclude.ending: The burden was pushed out of view.
exclude.text: The proposed arrangement leaves some people with a different experience without checking whether it meets their needs. Reopen the design before announcing a finished decision.
exclude.lesson: A convenient workaround is not automatically an accessible or acceptable one.
exclude.reflection: Whose input would change the decision, and what choice can you actually offer them?

overcommit.text: The budget or capacity commitment is unsupported. Correct the claim and seek an authorized, feasible arrangement before others rely on it.
overcommit.lesson: An attractive purpose does not justify invented resources or hidden limits.
overcommit.reflection: Which promise needs correction first, and who could be harmed by waiting?
